sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Unicode-aware reversal normally reverses the sequence of runes, not the UTF-8 bytes that encode them. Convert the string to `[]rune`, swap from both ends, and convert back.

Strings are immutable byte sequences. Rune conversion decodes code points into a mutable slice, and parallel assignment swaps each outside pair until the indexes meet.

For example, reversing `Go界` by runes produces `界oG`. Reversing its bytes moves pieces of the three-byte encoding for `界` and creates invalid UTF-8.

Rune reversal preserves code points, not necessarily user-perceived grapheme clusters. Emoji sequences and letters with combining marks can still be split if the product needs visual-character reversal.

Byte-wise reversal is safe only when the input contract guarantees one-byte characters, such as ASCII. For ordinary user text, rune-wise reversal is the clearer baseline.

Failures around reversing a string in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

UTF-8 represents common ASCII runes with one byte and many other runes with two to four. Reversing that byte order destroys the encoding inside each multi-byte rune. `utf8.ValidString` is a useful test signal, but the real fix is reversing the correct unit.
